# SK6060 — The interface's type parameter is invariant and need not be

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An interface whose type parameter appears only in output positions can declare it `out`, and every assignment its callers currently cannot write becomes legal without any of them changing.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Design |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

Variance is the one piece of an interface's design that costs the declarer nothing and is invisible until somebody needs it. `IReadOnlyList<out T>` is why `IReadOnlyList<string>` is an `IReadOnlyList<object>`; an interface that could have said the same thing and did not forces every consumer into a copy, a `Cast<T>()` or a second overload — and the consumer usually cannot tell that the restriction was accidental rather than meant. ⚠ **The declaration is the only place the question can be asked**, because the compiler will not infer it and nothing in a call site says "this would have worked".

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
interface IFactory<T> {
    T Create();
    IEnumerable<T> CreateMany(int count);
}

// IFactory<string> is not an IFactory<object>, for no reason.
```

Write:

```csharp
interface IFactory<out T> {
    T Create();
    IEnumerable<T> CreateMany(int count);
}
```

## When it does not fire

**The finding is the compiler's own variance-safety rule, run in reverse, and not an approximation of it.** Every occurrence of the parameter in every member signature is classified by position — a return type is covariant, a by-value or `in` parameter is contravariant, a `ref` or `out` parameter and a get-set property are invariant, an event is contravariant, a generic method's constraint is contravariant, and a base interface is covariant — and each occurrence is then composed through the declared variance of whatever generic type encloses it, flipping on a contravariant parameter and collapsing to invariant on an invariant one. That composition is what separates `IEnumerable<T> Get()`, which is reportable, from `List<T> Get()` and `Action<T> Get()`, which are not; all three look like the parameter sitting in a return type. ⚠ **Eight shapes were run through the real compiler before the algorithm was written**, and its answers agree with `CS1961` on all eight.

**Only interfaces, and only ones declared in source and not `partial`.** A delegate's type parameters admit exactly the same argument and are deliberately out of scope: the concept is the same, the decision to ship it is a separate one. A `partial` interface repeats its type parameter list on every declaration and C# requires the variance modifiers to match across all of them, so a fix that edits one part produces `CS0264`; the rule declines rather than emitting a multi-part edit.

⚠ **A parameter constrained to `struct` is declined even though `interface I<out T> where T : struct` compiles.** Variance exists to admit reference conversions and a value type admits none, so the suggestion would be true, accepted by the compiler, and worth nothing. The same goes for a parameter that occurs in no member signature at all: that is an unused type parameter, a different finding, and `out` on a phantom is noise.

**The parameter must occur at least once, and both directions are reported.** A parameter used only in output positions is offered `out`; one used only in input positions is offered `in`. A parameter that occurs only in invariant positions, or in both directions, is silent — there is nothing to suggest.

⚠ **The fix is `fixIsSafe: false` and the reason is not the source.** Adding a variance modifier is source-compatible for every consumer, and that is exactly what makes it easy to apply without thinking: it is **binary-breaking**. The type's metadata name is unchanged but its signature is not, so an already-compiled assembly referencing the old form fails to load against the new one. It also constrains every future member of the interface — a `void Set(T value)` that anyone might want to add later becomes a compiler error rather than a design discussion. Neither is visible in the diff.
